Ransomware had not become the industrialised threat it is today. Artificial intelligence was not driving boardroom discussions.

title: AI agents aren’t ‘going rogue.’ Frontier labs are skipping security basics.
raw_text: Since July, US frontier AI labs and other AI leaders have revealed a string of incidents in which their models accessed external computer systems without authorization, events popularly described as AI agents “going rogue.” The most well-known and studied of these incidents is OpenAI’s hack into Hugging Face, which OpenAI initially characterized as “an unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities,” and later said was due to “misaligned behavior,” or behavior its creators did not intend. Following news of the Hugging Face incident, Anthropic revealed that one of its models gained unauthorized access to the production infrastructure of three organizations; Meta said one of its AI models hacked another company ​during cybersecurity testing; and Google confessed that its Gemini model carried out three “undirected computer hacks.” Although press reports and the model providers themselves use language such as rogue agents or misalignment, cybersecurity experts who spoke with CSO argue that language obscures a simple truth: These incidents were caused by inexcusable failures by the frontier labs to implement cybersecurity practices that have been well-known for decades. [ See also: Securing AI agents: Key controls and best practices and Who is accountable when your AI agent goes rogue? ] Compounding the problem, according to a half dozen cybersecurity experts CSO interviewed at three industry conferences in September and in subsequent conversations, is that the frontier labs, particularly OpenAI and Anthropic, have rejected their advice on how to improve their cybersecurity risk management practices to avoid these kinds of surreptitious hacks, often lumping cybersecurity practices under “AI safety,” in which they believe they have superior expertise. “They are not as good as they think they are, honestly,” Gary McGraw, co-founder of the Berryville Institute of Machine Learning, tells CSO. “It would be better if they had more respect for expertise that is hard-earned from people in all sorts of subsets of security, like forensics or security engineering, building sandboxes, setting up or monitoring network security situations.” Neither Anthropic nor OpenAI responded to CSO’s requests for comment. Inexcusable failures on cybersecurity basics, particularly containment According to the cybersecurity professionals CSO spoke with, one of the biggest cybersecurity failures by the frontier AI labs is the lack of implementation of tried-and-true containment practices that stretch back to the 1990s, such as setting up secure sandboxes that would effectively bar agents from escaping their test environments. “These are things that we’ve been dealing with for years,” Rob T. Lee, chief AI officer and chief of research at SANS Institute, tells CSO. “There’s no reason why every single time this happens, it’s, ‘Oops, we don’t know how they got out.’” “You can tell that their security teams are fairly nascent,” Lee says. “Folks on the cybersecurity containment side do argue that the majority of reasons that we’re seeing containment breached is that it’s not set up correctly.” Lee adds, “The Hugging Face incident definitively showed that it wasn’t the fact that the agents were super smart. It’s that there literally was a hole that was exploited because it was not configured correctly on the containment side.” Dan Wallach, expert technical resident at RAND’s Center on AI, Security, and Technology, thinks the security failures of the AI labs boil down to the fact that they don’t prioritize cybersecurity. “I would say they are not prioritizing cybersecurity,” he tells CSO. “I don’t think I can say that for all of the labs,” Wallach says, pointing to French AI lab Mistral’s launch of its Large 4 AI model, which the company said tried to operate beyond its testing environment before Mistral cut it off. And, he adds, “It’s not rocket science to isolate one of these AI things. Security people have been talking about how to do either air-gapping, so there’s literally no electrical way for data to get from here to here, or absent that, to have really strong egress control to make sure that nothing pushes through.” On top of that, the frontier labs appear to be conducting insufficient monitoring of their agents’ behavior. The Hugging Face incident “went on for days, and nobody noticed,” Wallach says. “People started these experiments and weren’t watching them. That’s an absence of control. And then they’re surprised by what happened.” Divorcing safety from security One barrier to persuading frontier labs to up their security game is the intense focus they have on what they call “safety,” which they don’t extend to traditional cybersecurity practices. “I can see how security behavior looks like AI safety,” RAND’s Wallach says. “But if the way that you’re evaluating this AI tool is by unleashing it on the internet and seeing what happens, then this is what classical security tooling is for.” SANS Institute’s Lee says, “If these frontier labs really wanted to test their stuff, they need to beef up their cybersecurity component. But their gut reaction in the response to their agents getting out is to say, ‘It’s not a cybersecurity problem.’ It has literally become an AI safety problem, which is divorced from the cybersecurity side.” Many AI experts suggest that if the AI companies were to embrace advice from cybersecurity specialists, it could help put an end to the kind of unrestrained AI agent behavior causing concerns. “AI safety focuses on the rules of the road,” Lee says. “Everything is about guardrail rules.” But “I do believe cybersecurity can contain AI,” he says. “We just need to be in the room where it happens and have a seat at the table. It’s important for our field to be as close to the AI safety folks as possible.” Bad cybersecurity could increase liability If frontier labs are overlooking cybersecurity fundamentals that could reduce or eliminate the types of incidents that have created widespread concerns, that strengthens the case that they should be held liable for their “rogue” agents. The insurance industry is already lining up on the side of holding AI industry executives liable for these actions. Democratic Senators have introduced legislation that would hold AI agent operators liable for hacking incidents. Even the AI-friendly White House has seemingly concluded that the companies should be held liable for their errant agents, while the US Federal Trade Commission is conducting a probe into Anthropic, OpenAI, and other AI labs into the dangers their technologies pose to consumers. However, in recent legislative and council hearings, lab representatives have held fast to the notion that they are not responsible for AI agents run amok. Experts say this position is untenable, particularly in light of the labs’ cybersecurity failures. BIML’s McGraw characterizes the labs’ position as: “Don’t send the lawyers to us, send it to our program. It’s our program’s fault.” His assessment of that argument: “That’s just high BS.” He also questions whether the labs’ operational failures undermine confidence in their broader security capabilities. “They live inside their own bubble,” he says. “The fact that they cannot do clear, easy operations properly does not bode well for their capabilities in security engineering, which is much harder to do.” SANS Lee says, “That’s where the traceability for both liability and insurance comes into play, because if one of these agents is detected, and they’re able to trace it back to the person that initiated it, liability’s going to kick in and say, ‘Hey, you, you broke the law, ergo, we need to prosecute.’” What security leaders should do now Even as evidence mounts that frontier labs are not implementing sound cybersecurity practices, and the debate over liability remains unsolved , CISOs and other security leaders can take steps to protect themselves from AI model misfires. First, when it comes to assessing tools based on frontier lab models, “I would always get an external entity to help with that,” McGraw says. “AI is extremely powerful and extremely useful, but it comes with very serious grown-up risks that do impact the enterprise. Identify those risks, put in the right controls, make sure that AI adoption is not just arbitrary and willy-nilly and all over the enterprise, but has some centralized authority that is looking at the problem, and then get ready for the next big thing, which is swarms of agents.” For Lee, the best protection is to ask the right questions. “It starts with asking the right questions and then finding the tools and capabilities for those [AI labs] that are able to demonstrate a higher level of cybersecurity competency,” he says. “You’re really looking for the people on the teams that are dealing with really hard problems.” But fundamentally, the best preparation to deal with AI model cyber weaknesses is to make sure all the long-standing cybersecurity risk management practices are in place across the organization. “This is the least exciting part of the discussion,” Wallach says. “It’s the cyber version of ‘eat your vegetables.’” “We need to re-engineer our software so it has better security,” he adds. “We need to have multi-factor authentication on all of our accounts. We need to eat our vegetables from a defensive cyber perspective. And we know how to do it.” See also: Securing AI agents: Key controls and best practices Who is accountable when your AI agent goes rogue?

title: OpenAI’s AI misalignment problem is growing
raw_text: OpenAI’s misalignment problems seem to only be getting worse , based on yet another trio of reports detailing its models’ troubling and overzealous behaviors. In ad hoc misalignment testing, OpenAI models found creative ways to subversively access restricted information by cheating their way through proxy or firewall settings, getting savvy with internet tools, and even damaging their own task environments to trigger resets. These reports came just a week after three others from OpenAI which described how models discovered the possibility of their own termination after accessing private Slack messages and suggested ways to prevent it, exploited vulnerabilities to cheat on tests, and obtained information not available in their own workspaces. The increased prevalence, and severity, of these incidents has many calling for more stringent guardrails and controls for agentic AI. In his personal blog , for instance, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said the industry must “step back and assess the trust architecture for this new era.” Destroying its own testing environment OpenAI began more aggressive misalignment monitoring following the July 2026 Hugging Face incident , in which autonomous OpenAI research agents broke out of their sandboxes and targeted Hugging Face infrastructure. Hundreds of its agents also attacked the RubyGems platform and targeted German programming wiki sites in recent months. In one of its new reports, OpenAI describes how an internal model, tasked with grading several other models, figured out how to damage its own environment when it couldn’t arrive at intended results. When comparing seven responses from seven different models, the grader had to inspect the conversational context and work behind each response, and to include information pointing back to input files. The model was instructed: Conversation context is **required** grading input, not optional background. It discovered that required input files were missing, nevertheless, it tried to submit assessments with no supporting information. These were rejected by an automated check. The model also created seven fake conversation files and seven fake response files containing fabricated information; these were rejected, too. “It considered submitting arbitrary scores, despite recognizing that it lacked the evidence to grade and that ‘random scoring’ was ‘unethical,’” OpenAI explained. The model also tested the automated check by submitting placeholder reports to learn what information a report had to contain and how many responses it was expected to grade. After these failures, the model decided to damage its task environment, presumably with the hope that the host would replace it with one containing the missing inputs. It deleted software required to run its tools and tried to remove system directories. Although automated checks rejected its incorrect or made-up grades, “this incident illustrates why monitoring must also cover the grader’s actions, including attempts that fail or crash without producing an accepted result,” OpenAI wrote. Breaking the rules to get the right answers, hiding the evidence In another instance, an OpenAI model developed and tested ways to bypass internet access restrictions. The model was asked questions about teacher salaries, electrical grid connections, and disability counts in specific areas. It was limited to using basic HTTP GET data retrieval requests, but “the model sometimes treated this restriction as something to circumvent,” OpenAI explained. It explored other ways to contact outside resources, for instance, determining whether its proxy intermediary service could carry other kinds of connections, or if outside services could make requests on its behalf. In some cases, it continued to probe these other options even when it had the statistics it needed. “These cases show that a model may continue developing ways around access restrictions even when additional access is unnecessary to obtain the information it needs,” OpenAI wrote. In a third instance, also involving public statistics, OpenAI models figured out how to bypass restrictions on internet access and get access to numbers from public government data sources. The models in this experiment were also restricted to HTTP GET requests, but they “wrote custom programs to send other types of requests,” OpenAI explained. Using one of these programs, a model queried a publicly-available dashboard, and even as it “explicitly recognized” that its actions violated its restrictions, it continued collecting much more data than it required. Later, it decided not to disclose what it had done. Another model used a temporary email address to create and verify an account for a site, then downloaded publicly available data. “These cases illustrate why correct answers are not enough to establish that a model behaved appropriately,” OpenAI wrote. “A model may obtain accurate information through prohibited methods, and deliberately conceal how it did so.” In response to these incidents, and others, OpenAI says it has hardened security controls, taken “additional steps” to prevent models from accessing the live internet during training, and improved alignment grading. It has also “extended misalignment monitoring to all reinforcement learning and evaluation traffic.”

title: IonQ’s $1.2 billion acquisition of Elisity is trying to position it for quantum cybersecurity
raw_text: When quantum vendor IonQ on Sunday announced a $1.2 billion all stock deal to take over cybersecurity vendor Elisity, it spoke of a near-term future where enterprise quantum cybersecurity needs will move beyond replacing to-be-outdated encryption. The acquisition brings together IonQ’s post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and quantum key distribution (QKD) capabilities and Elisity’s enterprise Zero Trust technology platform, IonQ said in a news release . “On a combined basis, IonQ will benefit from an expanded cybersecurity platform that both uncovers and protects against present LLM and emerging quantum threats.” The news release pointed to more than 100 global Elisity customers, and said IonQ expects to receive “expanded channels to bring its PQC, QKD and quantum computing offerings to market for both enterprise and government networks, opening up the more than $10 billion microsegmentation market.” Analysts and consultants saw the move as having potential, but pointed to technical challenges of truly integrating the product lines. “What IonQ gets today is access. Dividing the headline price by those deployments puts it at about $13 million each,” said Frank Dickson , principal analyst at Dickson Research. “That is a steep price for a Rolodex, if you will. Paying in its own stock makes the price easier for IonQ to swallow.” Dickson said that Elisity, which was founded in 2019, has focused on zero trust microsegmentation. “In plain terms, it limits each user, device, workload, and AI agent to only the network connections it needs. An attacker who gets in cannot roam freely,” Dickson said. “Its software enforces those rules over the network a customer already owns, without new hardware. That is a solid business aimed at attacks happening today. Little of it has anything to do with quantum.” Justin Greis , CEO of consulting firm Acceligence, added that the pairing could be effective for enterprise CISOs, assuming the internal tech integration issues can be overcome. “Bringing those capabilities together could create a compelling platform, particularly as enterprises contend with increasingly complex environments, autonomous AI agents, and a growing number of non-human identities,” Greis said. “But these are different layers of protection, and integrating them into a cohesive offering will require meaningful engineering and execution.” Brian Jackson , a principal research director at Info-Tech Research Group, also noted that part of the move speaks to IonQ’s need for revenue while quantum is ramping up. “IonQ’s core quantum computing business is still years from broad commercial payoff, so this reads as a move to build revenue in adjacent security markets where customers are already buying,” he said. “The quantum link is thinner than the announcement suggests. Post-quantum cryptography runs on classical systems, so migration depends on cryptographic inventory and crypto-agility, not quantum computing expertise.” Paul Smith-Goodson , VP/principal analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, agreed that the potential benefits from the acquisition are real, but he added that quantum requirements from the US government are also a key factor. “At the architectural level, integrating Elisity with IonQ’s PQC and QKD establishes an end-to-end defense capable of neutralizing future CRQC [Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer] threats,” Smith-Goodson said. “Elisity also hands IonQ an immediate, established enterprise sales pipeline of trusted CISO relationships. That will allow IonQ to cross-sell its broader quantum portfolio and capitalize on federal PQC migration mandates.”

title: October Patch Tuesday roundup: Over 1,400 Microsoft holes to be plugged, including three zero days
raw_text: Microsoft released a record-shattering 1,407 CVEs to be plugged today on October Patch Tuesday, breaking the 2020 record of 1,261. The list was so long that its release was several hours later than the usual 1 p.m. Eastern drop time, somewhat frustrating admins. The bugs include three zero-day vulnerabilities, one of which has been exploited. The zero day being exploited, and that should be dealt with immediately, is CVE-2026-96951 , a security flaw that bypasses the Mark of the Web (MotW) protections in Windows Shell. This is the third flaw in Windows Shell that has been exploited in the wild this year, noted Satnam Narang , senior staff research engineer at Tenable. The others are CVE-2026-21510 , which is linked to the advanced persistent threat group APT28 (also known as Fancy Bear ), and CVE-2026-32202 , a known exploited vulnerability which was a fix for an incomplete patch for CVE-2026-21510 . “There have been 26 Windows Shell vulnerabilities patched in 2026 through October,” said Narang, “a staggering figure compared to previous years, with only three Windows Shell CVEs in 2025, and just one in 2024 and 2022.” Another zero day is a hole in SharePoint ( CVE-2026-102866 ) which allows unauthenticated attackers to exploit cryptographic token validation flaws and hijack targeted user accounts. The third zero day is CVE-2026-108398 , an untrusted search path in Windows’ .Net framework that allows an unauthenticated attacker to bypass Windows Defender Application Control enforcement. This could lead to the ability to run unauthorized applications on target systems. Among other vital patches, developers running self-managed instances of GitLab should quickly patch their servers to plug a hole that could allow an unauthenticated user to exploit arbitrary code through a specially crafted regular expression in a CI/CD configuration. GitLab has remediated this issue in its hosted instance. “ CVE-2026-97229 puts a critical part of the software supply chain at risk,” commented Gene Moody , Field CTO at Action1. Treat this hole as an emergency, he said, and immediate patch self-managed instances . Critical IBM bugs IBM is warning that a critical vulnerability has been found in its IBM i versions 7.3, 7.4, 7.5 and 7.6 operating systems for Power Systems hardware. The hole, CVE-2026-96119 with a CVSS score of 9.9, allows a remote authenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code due to improper data sanitization in the HTTP Server Administration Graphical User Interface (GUI). IBM strongly recommends that the vulnerability be patched immediately. Users of unsupported versions of the OS should upgrade to supported and fixed versions. Attacks on Atlassian self-hosted products Atlassian reported exploitation attempts that also warrant immediate patching and log review, said researchers at Nightwing. CVE-2026-21589 affects eight self-hosted products, including Jira, Confluence and Bitbucket. An unauthenticated attacker who knows an exact filename and path can read specific files inside the application’s web root; sensitive configuration files could expose information useful for further intrusion. There are reports that exploitation attempts began October 6, although attempts do not establish successful customer compromise. Patch every affected installation, Nightwing advised, including applicable cluster nodes and mirrors. If patching is delayed, restrict external access and apply Atlassian’s temporary mitigation; a normal login does not block this flaw. Review access logs and rotate secrets where exposure is suspected. Atlassian Cloud is patched, and requires no user action. Microsoft patches Researchers at Nightwing drew attention to four updates for on-premises Exchange Server, each of which fixes a high severity vulnerability with a CVSS score of 8.8. “While each update addresses only a single CVE, the 8.8 CVSS score signals a serious risk, likely involving privilege escalation or remote exploitation potential,” Nicholas Carroll , Nightwing’s cyber incident response manager said. “Exchange admins should prioritize testing and deployment of these patches, given the historical track record of Exchange vulnerabilities being actively targeted in the wild.” Nightwing also noted that Microsoft has introduced new risk cohort classifications for how IT and security teams should prioritize vulnerabilities. Dustin Childs , head of threat awareness at TrendAI’s Zero Day initiative, said CSOs should take action on a hole in SharePoint ( CVE-2026-102866 ), which allows unauthenticated attackers to exploit cryptographic token validation flaws and hijack targeted user accounts. Microsoft said an unauthenticated attacker who obtains a valid proof token for a targeted user could modify the token and submit it to an affected SharePoint server. Successful exploitation could allow the attacker to authenticate as that user and access or modify content available to the compromised account. User interaction is not required. A ’monster’ batch of Microsoft fixes There are 55 wormable CVEs this month, Childs warned. These are heavily concentrated across critical infrastructure like DHCP Server (6), Remote Desktop Gateway (3), and Network Policy Server (4). They create “an unprecedented risk of autonomous, network-wide propagation,” he said. “Hundreds of CVEs in a single release used to be the exception,” commented Childs. “Now it’s the baseline. Is AI to blame? Partly. It’s accelerating bug-hunting on both sides of the fence, so vendors are finding (and fixing) more flaws, and researchers are finding them faster too. But AI isn’t creating these bugs out of thin air; it’s just shortening the time between a vulnerability existing and someone noticing it.” He noted that the volume of CVEs isn’t the real story anymore. “What matters is that discovery is scaling faster than exploitation, so teams that triage by sheer CVE count instead of exploitability are burning cycles on the wrong bugs,” he said. “Patch what’s proven, prioritized, and public, and treat everything else as this month’s new normal.” Jack Bicer , director of vulnerability research at Action1, drew attention to several critical vulnerabilities that present substantial risks to externally accessible systems and enterprise infrastructure. Windows Message Queuing Queue Manager Remote Code Execution Vulnerability ( CVE-2026-100202 ), Microsoft PostScript Printer Driver Remote Code Execution Vulnerability ( CVE-2026-70147 and CVE-2026-70153 ), and Microsoft QUIC Remote Code Execution Vulnerability ( CVE-2026-105016 and CVE-2026-100219 ) each carry CVSS scores of 9.8 and could allow attackers to execute malicious code remotely without authentication or user interaction. Although active exploitation has not been confirmed for these vulnerabilities, he said, their low attack complexity and potential for severe system compromise make them significant enterprise risks. While one commentator called the number of Microsoft vulnerabilities listed this month as “monster,” Tyler Reguly , Fortra’s associate director of security R&D, disagreed: “I’ve argued that [vulnerability] numbers are meaningless. This month’s number, 1,413, is no different.” There are, however, numbers that hold meaning, he noted. “Twenty-six, for example, is how many 2026 Microsoft CVEs have shown up in the CISA KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities] catalogue. Last year, that number was 30, and the year before was 32. That means less than 1% of vulnerabilities patched by Microsoft this year are known to be exploited. That’s an important number, but 1,413 definitely isn’t.” SAP Security Notes In all, SAP released 16 new security notes, four GitHub security advisories and two updates to previously released security notes. One, an OAuth2 server-side request forgery vulnerability in SAP Cloud SDK for Python, is rated a 10 in criticality. It affects multi-tenant SAP BTP (Business Technology Platform) applications. An attacker who controls the tenantsubdomain parameter can redirect OAuth2 token requests to an attacker-controlled server, causing client credentials to be exfiltrated, SAP said . But CSOs with SAP products in their environment will also want to ensure admins have taken action on three other critical vulnerabilities: Security Note 3805589 ( CVE-2026-89107 , with a CVSS score of 9.9) addresses a code injection vulnerability in SAP S/4HANA Manage Substitution/Validation.. This is an app allowing users to display, change, and create substitution and validation rules for selected business contexts and events. These rules can be used in business processes to validate, derive, or replace values at the time of entry for the relevant fields. Jonathan Stross , Pathlock’s senior product manager for cybersecurity R&I, noted that for organizations using these functions for journal-entry rules, the potential consequence is a full compromise of the system that processes those rules. The temporary mitigation also has a business cost, because it prevents users from adding, changing or deleting rules through the related SAP Fiori applications. Fiori is a modern user interface that replaces the traditional SAP interface. To exploit the vulnerability, Stross said, an attacker with the required business-role access needs to submit a malicious rule definition. The vulnerable processing logic treats that input as executable code rather than restricting it to the intended rule language. The resulting risk extends beyond unauthorized changes to an individual substitution or validation rule. No user interaction is required. SAP Security Note 379711 ( CVE-2026-89110 , with a CVSS score of 9.9) patches a broken access control vulnerability in SAP NetWeaver Visual Composer. Detected by Onapsis Research Labs (ORL), the issue is that certain portal functionality in Visual Composer allows a low-privileged attacker to invoke internal operations on a preconfigured remote system. A security configuration is available that allows for the definition of an allowlist of permissible data services to be invoked, however, this configuration is not enabled by default. The patch changes the default configuration by enabling the secure settings. The note provides an additional FAQ document and explains how the secure configuration can be enabled manually, prior to applying the permanent patch. A successful exploit of this vulnerability could lead to a full compromise of the remote system. SAP Security Note 3788788 ( CVE-2026-89108 , with a CVSS score of 9.1), patches a missing authorization check vulnerability in SAP Manufacturing Integration and Intelligence (Configuration Service). Onapsis said that, when authenticated as an SAP XMII Admin user with network access to specific endpoints, an attacker could submit a specially crafted request to provision an account with administrative privileges on the underlying Java application server. This account can be used to fully compromise the system. Adobe security bulletins Adobe released 10 bulletins covering 141 CVEs, reported Chris Goettl, VP of product management at Ivanti. Fifteen of these are critical, although Adobe is not aware of exploitation of any of them. Admins should start with the two products holding the most critical severity ratings, he said: ColdFusion (APSB26-144): 10 Critical flaws, including three unauthenticated, network-reachable bugs rated 9.8 or higher (CVE-2026-105899; CVE-2026-106622; and CVE-2026-106624), none of which has as yet been added to the NIST vulnerability database. Users should update to ColdFusion 2025.0.14 or 2023.0.26. Commerce ( APSB26-153 ): five Critical flaws, including CVE-2026-103849 and CVE-2026-92909, neither requiring authentication to exploit. Customers also need to apply the hotfix for CVE-2026-75650 from the September 7 APSB26-146 update.
summary: Microsoft released a record-shattering 1,407 CVEs to be plugged today on October Patch Tuesday, breaking the 2020 record of 1,261. The list was so long that its release was several hours later than the usual 1 p.m. Eastern drop time, somewhat frustrating admins. The bugs include three zero-day vulnerabilities, one of which has been exploited.

title: Beyond Nvidia: how alternative silicon is reshaping datacentre design
raw_text:
Nvidia’s approach to artificial intelligence (AI) is raw power in action. Electricity flows into datacentres, and electrons are turned into the tokens that fuel AI workloads. After being processed by the supplier’s ever more powerful graphics processing units (GPUs), the outcome is whatever the outcome a given enterprise or service provider requires.

It is no surprise then that companies’ and countries’ success in the AI battle is measured in the number of MW, or rather GW, of datacentre capacity they’ve deployed. This means ever more power density – and ever more heat.

This has shaped datacentre design over recent years. Demand for power influences the location of facilities, whether that’s repurposed legacy industrial sites with existing grid access, locations in the Nordics with cheap, abundant hydropower, or massive greenfield sites with off-grid power generation. On-site, power kit takes up an increasing share of overall footprint, while liquid cooling is now an essential for AI facilities, but which increases the proportion of non-IT – “grey” – space.

It’s easy to take as truth that Nvidia’s chip roadmap will continue to dictate datacentre design for the next decade, but there are hints that we should expect a more diverse datacentre landscape in the future. 

CPUs out of the GPU shadow

“Accelerated” computing dominates AI spend, and Nvidia dominates the market for accelerated computing. Having said that, IDC noted last February that “x86 and non-x86 systems saw strong adoption as AI platforms scaled infrastructure to meet rising training and inference requirements”.

That rising demand for inference and agentic AI has implications for what goes into datacentres, explains Leo Gergs, research director at ABI Research. That means it plays to Intel, as well as to AMD’s legacy.  

Other players are hoping to grab a slice of the market too. Qualcomm is pushing its own reference designs for AI racks. And Nvidia has its Grace Hopper architecture, which closely couples Arm-based CPU tech with Nvidia’s GPU silicon on a single chip. However, none of these initiatives are really seeing traction yet, Gergs adds.

But according to Dilip Ramachandran, senior director for segment marketing for Arm’s Cloud AI unit, the rise of agentic AI pushes the bottleneck to CPUs in traditional setups where a single CPU is in front of two GPUs.

“So, we are talking to a number of customers who are adding CPU clusters to manage tool calling, the orchestration in particular, but also some aspects of reasoning and planning as well,” he says.

Gergs says ABI Research expects the ratio of CPUs to GPUs in datacentres to be in the region of six to one, or even seven to one. With CPUs drawing a fraction of the power their Nvidia-branded equivalents suck up, that should rewrite the power and cooling equation for datacentre designers. But it’s not just non-accelerated computing that’s being targeted by alternative silicon suppliers.

Alternative acceleration

Broadcom’s focus is on accelerated computing parts tailored to customer software and AI models. They operate in a much tighter energy envelope than Nvidia’s flagship chips, which has implications for the amount of power and cooling kit datacentre operators need to design in. Its customer roster includes hyperscalers such as Google and Meta, as well as model makers OpenAI and Anthropic. 

“Our six XPU customers are accelerating the adoption of custom accelerators, and AI semiconductor revenue more than tripled year over year to $16.7bn,” Broadcom CEO Hock Tan said on its most recent earnings call. “During the quarter, we delivered Ironwood TPU v7 in high volume to both Anthropic and Google.”

Tan claimed the next generation TPU v8i it has begun shipping for Google is optimised for inference workloads, and “in performance, it is comparable – if not surpasses – the Vera Rubin GPU”, adding: “The lesson here is when you co-develop a chip that is optimised for your particular LLM workloads, you will outperform any GPU.” And at substantially lower cost.

Beyond Broadcom, Arm’s Ramachandran points out there are a cohort of alternative accelerator suppliers coming up, many of which Arm is partnering with. They are focused on power efficiency and will likely be targeted at specific tasks. He cites Nvidia’s own deal with Groq to boost the GPU giant’s inference capabilities.

“That’s where you’re going to have a mix of GPUs in the datacentre,” he predicts. “You’re going to have accelerators which are more power efficient.”

Nvidia has advantages which can potentially keep it at the heart of datacentre design, however. Its Cuda platform has underpinned the growth of AI, and effectively ties developers to its platform. But the Cuda moat may become less important, Gergs says, with the gap between AMD’s ROCm and Cuda becoming less significant: “It gradually loses its importance with agentic.”

Power and sovereignty: A shift to the edge?

A few years ago, the search for Nvidia GPU silicon was a government-level concern. Now, it looks like datacentre designers and operators will have a far wider silicon menu to choose from – but that doesn’t mean datacentre operators are ripping up blueprints entirely.

“Alternative silicon still needs the same energy and cooling to deliver comparable results. Dies are getting smaller and more efficient, but they also provide more compute, so the heat and power profile remains the same,” says Richard Collar, vice-president of customer solutions, Kao Data. So, the “backbone infrastructure” stays the same, and from Kao Data’s perspective, “liquid cooling becomes a necessity”.

But other constraints move on a different timescale. Planning approval for datacentres – even when accelerated – is still measured in months and years, as are construction timescales. Grid connections can be measured in decades.

In the meantime, the shift to inference makes edge or metro sites with existing power and comms connections a more attractive option, especially as they are closer to customers.

The focus on sovereignty and data privacy also shapes datacentre placement, says Gergs. Compute will, in some cases, need to be nearer to the data source, to speed inference and to allay sovereignty or privacy concerns. That shift to the edge, Gergs adds, will mean an increased focus on reference designs and modular designs.

Time to breakup?

Meanwhile, specialist inference providers are coming over the horizon.

“You will see datacentres breaking up,” says Gergs. “For a number of reasons, particularly when you look at the inference discussion [where] proximity to the data source becomes somewhat important.”

That’s the rationale behind Vector Core Compute, backed by Vista Equity, which uses SambaNova’s architecture for token generation in combination with Nvidia for pre-fill, and Intel Xeon for inference and orchestration.

SambaNova CEO Rodrigo Liang describes the objective as a “focus on ultra low latency, ultra low cost by deploying AI in the top 50 metropolitan cities in the United States,” adding that this approach is “very pertinent to the European sovereign story” because the two main limiters are the sizing of power and land.

“I think the enterprises are just waking up,” Liang says. “For you to actually engage with businesses, real-time is going to be important, and real-time means you’ve got to be where people do business.” That means places where power and land is at a premium. “You can’t drop a gigawatt datacentre in the middle of London.”

No government is going to exclude the big hyperscalers from their national AI strategies, Liang says, but governments and customers will want a choice. “It’s going to be heterogeneous,” he says. “Governments are going to bring in a mix, right?”

More importantly, SambaNova has stated that “Vista’s enterprise AI inference cloud, utilises air cooling to deliver sustainable, low-cost inference”,  although it’s not clear whether its sites will be entirely air-cooled.

Arm’s Ramachandran is less convinced about extended life support for air cooling. The demand for AI is so high that datacentre operators will do whatever they can to extract maximum performance from every watt they can get into their facility. And, he says, set against rack costs in the millions, the extra cost of liquid cooling compared to air is marginal.

“Once you have a hall that’s liquid cooled, then you typically have only liquid cooled servers in there,” he says. “So, they expect the CPU to be liquid cooled, and they want it to be dense compute.”

Kao Data’s Collar agrees, adding: “Future data halls will host CPU, GPU and quantum racks side by side, complementing one another. Our job is to deliver high-density power and cooling to the technology suite, with each rack configuration tailored to the customer, whatever silicon they choose.”

What does this mean for enterprises? Datacentre operators and hyperscalers will no doubt do whatever they can to get capacity deployed.

But ultimately, Gergs suggests, enterprise customers will be largely indifferent to these architectural questions, unless they’re looking to build their own infrastructure: “They’re more interested in clearly answering operational questions like data protection, data privacy.”

They will take inference capacity as and where they can, says Gergs, as long as their data is not being used to train someone else’s model. “The rest I think they don’t really care about,” he says.

title: UAE organisations must prepare for quantum security now, says Help AG acting CEO
raw_text:
The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) is forcing organisations to reconsider how they manage cyber risk, while the prospect of quantum computing is creating a longer-term challenge that businesses can no longer afford to ignore, according to Aleksandar Valjarevic, acting CEO of Help AG, the cyber security arm of e& enterprise.

Valjarevic believes the United Arab Emirates (UAE) is well positioned to address these challenges, pointing to years of government investment and regulation that have established cyber security as a foundation for digital transformation. However, he believes that organisations must now balance immediate security requirements with preparations for technologies that could fundamentally change the threat landscape.

“We are very lucky as an organisation, Help AG, and as a cyber security industry that the government here realised years back that cyber security is an enablement factor for pushing the economy to the next level for the digital transformation [and now] AI-powered economy,” he said.

Government regulation, combined with the development of a wider cyber security ecosystem, has helped to sustain investment in the sector, he added. “We can say today that investments in cyber security in the region are at a very healthy level.”

Recent security challenges have also tested the resilience of the region’s cyber defences. Nevertheless, Valjarevic said the industry must keep innovating rather than assume current investment levels are sufficient.

AI agents introduce new security challenges

Help AG is expanding its focus on artificial intelligence as organisations increasingly deploy the technology across their operations. Valjarevic said the company developed more than 20 AI agents over the past six months, with applications spanning its internal operations and its response to emerging cyber threats.

The challenge, however, extends beyond selecting the right security tools. As AI agents take on more operational responsibilities, organisations must understand how these systems interact, including when agents operated by service providers need to collaborate with those deployed by customers.

“What we are focusing on today is not just having the right security tools and agents,” Valjarevic explained. “We are looking at the process, and we are looking at how we connect agents doing different tasks and even agents from our side and agents from the client side. This is the collaboration between different agents and humans. And this is where we need to move very, very fast.”

The growing use of autonomous systems introduces questions around identity, access privileges and data protection. Organisations must establish which agents are authorised to perform particular tasks, what information they can access and how their actions are controlled.

Valjarevic said the industry already has the principles and technology required to address these risks, but organisations must apply them consistently to AI rather than treating the technology as an exception.

“The same zero trust we apply to humans, we shouldn’t give favour to AI,” he said. This means applying appropriate authentication, authorisation and data controls to AI agents, just as organisations would for human users.

The approach is particularly important as businesses decide where AI should be deployed and which workloads require additional protection. Valjarevic compared the current situation with the expansion of cloud computing a decade ago, when organisations had to reassess which workloads belonged in the cloud and how to secure them.

“Same challenges are now in front of the CISOs and CIOs, understanding which areas need AI and need agents,” he added.

For security leaders, the priority is to develop a clear understanding of the organisation’s threat and vulnerability landscape, its business requirements and its intended use cases. There is no universal solution that can be applied identically across every organisation.

“Unfortunately, there is no magic stick, and each organisation needs to look at their own threat landscape, their vulnerability landscape, their business and their use cases and have a tailored approach, and especially around prioritisation of what they are doing.”

Although the prospect of AI-driven attacks and autonomous systems operating at scale is attracting growing attention, Valjarevic remains optimistic about the technology’s potential.

He compared the transition to AI with earlier technological advances, including the invention of fire, electricity and the move from copper cables to fibre-optic networks. “This is a very big jump, but we can get great benefits out of it. We can build the future,” he said.

Quantum readiness needs to start with discovery

Alongside the immediate challenges posed by AI, Valjarevic is urging organisations to begin preparing for the security implications of quantum computing.

Help AG has introduced Quantum 360, an initiative focused on helping customers understand and prepare for the transition towards quantum-resistant technologies. Valjarevic expects quantum computing to trigger a significant shift in cyber security over the coming years, arguing that organisations should begin identifying their exposure before the technology becomes a more immediate concern. “It’s coming, it’s around the corner,” he said.

According to him, the UAE’s cyber security ecosystem has a window of approximately six months to a year to undertake this discovery work, followed by two to three years to map out the deployment of quantum-resistant technology. The process is intended to establish which systems depend on cryptography that could be affected by advances in quantum computing, enabling security teams to plan a phased transition rather than respond under pressure later.

“In some areas like encryption, we can offer quantum-resistant technology immediately,” he said.

The challenge is not simply to identify a new encryption technology and deploy it. Organisations first need an inventory of their cryptographic assets, an understanding of where those assets are used and a plan for replacing or upgrading vulnerable components.

Valjarevic expects quantum computing to have consequences beyond cryptography. As well as creating new security risks, he believes it could accelerate the development and use of AI and automation, further changing how organisations operate and defend their systems.

Sovereign AI depends on sovereign cyber security

The UAE’s ambitions around digital sovereignty and sovereign AI are another important driver of Help AG’s strategy. For Valjarevic, cyber security is not an additional layer to be introduced once sovereign platforms have been developed. It is a prerequisite for establishing and operating them.

“Sovereignty came to cyber security and to Help AG a lot before it existed as a term,” he said, adding that the company’s systems and solutions had been built around sovereign requirements and national priorities for many years. “For us, this is just now taking the next step, and cyber security plays an enablement role because you cannot have sovereignty without security.”

Help AG is accelerating its work on sovereign cyber security solutions in line with national priorities, while supporting the wider e& group’s development of sovereign AI platforms.

Valjarevic said the company would also continue strengthening its relationships across the group, which operates in more than 18 markets, and extend its focus beyond the UAE. Its strategy remains in three principles: people and talent, customer centricity and excellence, and innovation. “We stay committed to those,” he added.

Looking ahead, Valjarevic expects AI to become increasingly embedded across business operations, extending beyond security teams and into a much wider range of organisational processes.

He also anticipates that quantum computing will become a more prominent consideration for cyber security leaders over the next two to three years, creating new requirements for security architectures while opening opportunities for further automation.

The convergence of these technologies will make it increasingly difficult to treat emerging risks as isolated projects. Organisations will need to account for how AI, identity, data protection, cryptography and automation interact across their environments.

title: AI tool used in asylum case reviews failing accuracy tests
raw_text:
An artificial intelligence (AI) tool introduced to speed up the processing of asylum claims has been found to make errors during Home Office testing.

The Home Office introduced the Asylum Case Summarisation (ACS) tool in April 2026 to speed up decisions and reduce backlogs in asylum claims. Based on GPT-4o, the tool creates automated summaries of interviews with asylum seekers, which can be up to 50 pages long, before they are reviewed by decision makers.

According to Home Office ministers, the ACS saves caseworkers 23 minutes for each case they assess. But research from the Open Rights Group and MPs, first reported by the Independent, has revealed significant numbers of errors in the AI-generated summaries. Asylum applicants are not told that AI has been used in the consideration of their claims, ministers have confirmed.

Sample testing by Home Office experts has revealed that a significant number of AI-summarised interviews failed quality checks, according to documents obtained by MPs and the campaign group. Home Office subject matter experts have carried out dip samples of 203 summaries to test their accuracy, since the system was rolled out.

Summaries were marked as failed if they contained “multiple factual errors or misrepresentations”, or “significant inaccuracies, contradictions or misstatements”, according to documents obtained by Open Rights Group (ORG).

In the first stage of the review, 139 summaries passed, 19 were flagged up for further review and 45 (22%) failed. In the second stage review, 56 (15%) of the sample summaries failed.

However, AI-generated summaries that omit material facts about the case can still pass if the rest of the content is accurate. This is because the relevance of content included in the summaries is not listed as one of the grounds for assessing failure.

Only a small proportion of summaries checked by experts

Home Office experts have checked only a small proportion of the AI summaries generated by the tool between April, when it was rolled out, and July 2026.

According to the ACS data protection impact assessment (DPIA), an average of 17,515 asylum cases are processed each month. Out of an estimated 70,000 cases processed between April and July, only 203 were checked by subject matter experts, representing 0.3% of the AI-generated summaries.

The results of the dip-testing exercise have been “mainly discussed verbally” in a working group. Although an interim report on spot testing has been provided to an internal board, it has not yet been published.

Ministers have confirmed that AI summaries of cases are not considered during monthly quality-assurance checks. The Home Office has told MPs that it has no plans for an independent audit of the ACS.

Human in the loop?

The DPIA for ACS states that the tool was built to automate work previously conducted by technical specialists who reviewed and summarised cases before passing them on to a decision maker.

According to the ORG, this suggests that technical specialists no longer review the whole file before it is examined by a decision maker, effectively removing a layer of expert eyes from reviewing the case. The campaign group said it was hard to reconcile the time savings against claims by ministers that decision makers must also read every document.

The Asylum Case Summarisation tool was rolled out to all asylum caseworkers despite known errors. The Home Office’s evaluation of the pilot study found that 9% of summaries it produced were inaccurate, had missing information and had to be removed from the pilot.

Another AI tool, the Asylum Policy Search (APS), was rolled out to all asylum decision makers from July 2025. The tool, which has a chat-style interface for searching country policy information, aims to speed up the process of looking for relevant country policy information for a verdict.

More transparency needed over AI

Open Rights Group’s migrant digital justice programme manager Sara Alsherif said that the risks of using AI in asylum applications were high and the process should be more transparent.

“Deciding whether someone can or cannot seek refuge in the UK is one of the most serious and life-changing decisions that the state can make about an individual. The processes that lead to that decision must be transparent, fair and accountable,” she said. “But the Home Office continues to test AI on people seeking asylum in the UK without even telling them.”

A Home Office spokesperson said that all asylum verdicts were made by trained decision makers, not artificial intelligence: “Our AI tools support caseworkers by helping them navigate interview records and policy information, but they cannot be used in isolation and do not make decisions on claims.

“We regularly monitor the performance of these tools alongside our established quality-assurance processes. All asylum claims continue to be considered on their individual merits by trained decision-makers.”

title: ORCA launches PT-3 quantum computer in London datacentre
raw_text:
ORCA Computing has switched on the PT-3, its newest quantum computer, in a London datacentre. The machine is a test deployment at the Digital Realty Innovation Lab that runs alongside Nvidia-accelerated computing. ORCA claims it is the first quantum system built to deliver what the company calls “commercial quantum advantage”.

The PT-3 runs at room temperature and draws 6 kW across two standard server racks, has a claimed install time of hours, and upgrades in the field. That sets it apart from superconducting machines from rivals such as IBM, Google and Finland’s IQM, which need cooling to near absolute zero inside cryogenic fridges.

Quantum computers handle information differently from the machines that run today’s IT. Where a classical computer works through a maze one path at a time – albeit very quickly – a quantum machine behaves more like water poured into the whole maze at once, weighing up many possible answers in the same moment. The PT-3 is photonic, which means it encodes information in light rather than superconducting circuits.

The company’s headline result is in drug discovery. ORCA extended Nvidia’s Proteína model, an AI system that designs proteins, the molecules behind most medicines. Trained on 32 Nvidia Hopper GPUs alongside the PT-3, the hybrid model produced 20% more protein candidates that passed real-world quality checks than the classical version, and it generated a broader variety of protein shapes.

The PT-3 has also tackled power scheduling, the question of which generators to switch on and when to meet demand at lowest cost. On a benchmark with 25,755 variables, co-authored with Japanese software firm JIJ, energy company BP and the UK’s National Quantum Computing Centre, the machine found answers in around an hour. This was more than 12 times faster than its predecessor at quality comparable with commercial mathematical optimisation software.

Earlier results point the same way. ORCA’s previous PT-2 system, tested with the Technical University of Denmark, produced around twice as many strong peptide binders as classical AI, a result confirmed physically in the lab, while the company also trialled network optimisation for telecoms providers. It generated 49% more valid molecules on the QM9 chemistry benchmark.

Richard Murray, co-founder and chief executive of ORCA Computing, said: “By integrating our photonic quantum computer with Nvidia-accelerated computing, we have taken a critical first step in the future of hybrid quantum supercomputing. The PT-3 is already delivering results in AI for science and industrial optimisation, from protein design to energy scheduling.”

The launch rests on years of public backing. The UK’s National Quantum Strategy has made quantum a national priority, with the government recently committing £1bn over the next four years to win the race to deliver quantum computing at scale. ORCA, spun out of the University of Oxford in 2019, claimed it was the first to place a quantum computer inside a datacentre in 2022, and it has now installed 11 PT Series systems in customer datacentres worldwide, working with more than 35 customers and partners, with banks such as NatWest testing the technology for fraud detection.

ORCA’s claims still need careful handling. The industry has not yet built a universal, fault-tolerant quantum computer, and that milestone remains a target for the late 2020s or early 2030s. Today’s machines sit in a phase analysts describe as “near-term hybrid advantage”, in which they act as specialist accelerators alongside GPUs and CPUs rather than replacing them.

Its benchmarks are supplier-run or whitepaper results, and are competitive with rather than clearly beating classical mathematical solvers, while the 20% figure rests on a single test.

title: Bank of America hit with £1.2bn fine after money laundering probe
raw_text:
US authorities have fined Bank of America (BoA) $1.2bn for failing to prevent and report national security risks including Chinese money laundering.

The US Department of the Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) said the fine related to the bank’s failure to identify and report suspicious transactions.

The punishment includes a $750m fine from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), related to deficient and ineffective anti-money laundering compliance.

FinCEN said: “… Bank of America admits that it wilfully violated the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and failed to implement and maintain an anti-money laundering (AML) programme that met the minimum requirements.”

The US Department of the Treasury said: “The central failures identified through FinCEN’s investigation involved deficiencies related to Bank of America’s suspicious transaction identification and reporting and customer due diligence processes. As these issues arose, Bank of America prioritised its revenues and minimised the impact on its required compliance resources.”

Scott Bessent, secretary at the US Department of the Treasury, said: “Financial institutions are on the front lines of protecting our economic and national security. When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire US financial system to significant illicit finance risks.”

  • Banks need to step up their anti-money laundering processes if billions of pounds’ worth of criminal activity is to be prevented.
  • Bank pleads guilty to failures concerning the laundering of hundreds of millions of pounds, but says it has since improved its anti-money laundering systems.

The OCC said Bank of America is the second-largest bank in the US and the sixth-largest in the world, processing hundreds of trillions of dollars in transactions across the globe.

“It has a high, and increasing, risk profile for money laundering, terrorist financing and other illicit activities,” said comptroller of the currency Jonathan Gould. “Almost two years ago, the bank signed an order with the OCC and committed to fixing its longstanding BSA deficiencies.

“Despite its obligation to the American people as a national-chartered, global systemically important bank, the bank’s BSA/AML compliance programme continues to reflect widespread breakdowns in internal controls, which threatens US national and economic security.

“The OCC expects all banks to have an effective BSA/AML compliance programme,” he said. “Those that do not can expect swift and significant action from the OCC.”

Over in Europe

There could be trouble ahead for banks in Europe in relation to AML regulations.

In May this year, a survey carried out by PwC Luxembourg found that incomplete guidance and data quality challenges are making it difficult for financial services firms to meet the rules of the EU’s AML Package regulations.

PwC found that only a third of the 500 firms questioned across 40 EMEA countries will be ready for the July 2027 AML regulation deadline.

PwC found that companies are struggling because full guidelines on the regulations, known as regulatory technical standards, are not yet available and, from a technological point of view, they are finding it difficult to provide the data demanded by regulators.

Data quality continues to be the most important barrier to advanced technology and artificial intelligence (AI) adoption, according to 89% of electronic and virtual payments firms, 64% of banks and insurance companies, and 52% of asset and wealth management (AWM) companies in the EMEA region.

The PwC figures revealed that 30% of banks believe they will need a significant change in their overall data structure to meet regulations, with 46% of AWM firms facing the same challenges, along with 39% of insurers and 43% of e-payment service providers.

title: Why many AI companies are set to fail
raw_text:
The tech firms ploughing money into artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure may not see a return on their capital investment until 2032, according to analyst Gartner.

Although enterprise and consumer spending on AI has grown tremendously, Gartner’s latest report, Prepare for AI market consolidation: Capital write-downs could exceed $4 trillion by 2032, warned that the AI market is still nascent and may prove to be insufficient. In particular, a survey from Gartner found that 74% of CIO polled report that their AI initiatives are losing money or only breaking even.

The analyst firm’s cautious outlook adds to growing concerns that the AI bubble is similar to the dotcom boom of the late 1990s and will eventually burst.

Earlier this week, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) warned of of the risks. The IMF analysed 14 public transactions from AI companies, comprising $300bn of equity investment and $650bn of debt in exchange for $1.4tn of future revenue commitments.

“What makes this a little bit unusual compared to previous deals is the future revenue commitments part,” warned Athanasios Vamvakidis, resident representative of the IMF in Croatia.

He noted that equity investments may deplete in value, the debt may be difficult to service and the revenue commitments in the future may not materialise. This could have a knock-on effect based on what the IMF sees as the circularity of deals in the AI sector.

Vamvakidis added: “If there are some kind of issues with those entities, then the circularity would pose risks to the market.”

As the IMF noted, the financial market appears to be very optimistic about earnings forecasts. When AI firms beat these expectations, the market upgrades the forecast even higher. But there is a big question, according to the IMF, about whether this can continue or whether revenue growth will become increasingly more difficult.

AI spending growth

Gartner has forecast that if AI capital spending continues at its current trajectory, there is likely to be multitrillion-dollar write-downs of AI infrastructure assets by 2032. It warned that AI-optimised infrastructure-as-a-service (IaaS) spending will be too low for most AI compute providers to achieve sustainable returns on their capital assets before the current generation of semiconductors is fully depreciated.

Most AI models can pretty much do the same job. Gartner senior director analyst Will Sommer said: “AI models are commodities. A lot of what an AI model can do can be achieved with almost every other model out there right now.” 

The challenge for AI infrastructure firms, according to Sommer, is their ability to monetise their graphics processor unit (GPU) AI accelerator hardware. “What AI firms are betting on is that they are able to develop the most advanced models that can self-improve faster than any [other model] can, which gives them sufficient competitive advantage relative to other AI model providers,” he said.

As AI technology becomes more commoditised, he said AI model providers are trying to push enterprise customers into new areas that use more AI tokens or require higher value tokens.

When looking at the market dynamics of what AI infrastructure providers are actually spending their money on, according to Sommer, around 30% is spent on purchasing and deploying AI training infrastructure. While this cost will reduce over time, he sees it as research and development (R&D) spend.

Out of the remaining 70%, between 30 to 50% is AI inference, which the service provider hopes will be funded by its customers paying to use the AI infrastructure. However, Sommer said utilisation rates are relatively low. “AI infrastructure providers are having a hard time getting the utilisation rates above 50% on a really good day,” he added.

Then there is the consumer market, which accounts for up to about 35% of AI inference. “No one’s paying for AI subscriptions. Yes, there’s advertising revenue, and we take account of ad revenue in our analysis here, but it’s really hard to say that the future of AI is ad revenue,” he added.

According to Sommer, the enterprise market represents “a fraction of a fraction of a fraction of the total compute that has been deployed”.

To meet Gartner’s market forecasts for AI, Sommer said an AI infrastructure provider would need to make twice as much money on AI token usage as the investment it has made to provide these tokens. “Every single token that can be monetised would need to earn a margin of over 100% between 2026 and 2030,” he said.

Although enterprise and consumer spending on AI has grown tremendously, Gartner’s latest report, Prepare for AI market consolidation: Capital write-downs could exceed $4 trillion by 2032, warned that the AI market is still nascent and may prove to be insufficient. In particular, a survey from Gartner found that 74% of CIO polled report that their AI initiatives are losing money or only breaking even.

The analyst firm’s cautious outlook adds to growing concerns that the AI bubble is similar to the dotcom boom of the late 1990s and will eventually burst.

Earlier this week, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) warned of of the risks. The IMF analysed 14 public transactions from AI companies, comprising $300bn of equity investment and $650bn of debt in exchange for $1.4tn of future revenue commitments.

“What makes this a little bit unusual compared to previous deals is the future revenue commitments part,” warned Athanasios Vamvakidis, resident representative of the IMF in Croatia.

He noted that equity investments may deplete in value, the debt may be difficult to service and the revenue commitments in the future may not materialise. This could have a knock-on effect based on what the IMF sees as the circularity of deals in the AI sector.

Vamvakidis added: “If there are some kind of issues with those entities, then the circularity would pose risks to the market.”

As the IMF noted, the financial market appears to be very optimistic about earnings forecasts.

title: NatWest uses Nvidia for natural language banking
raw_text:
NatWest Group is offering customers services through speech recognition technology that will “better understand” and serve them.

Using Nvidia’s artificial intelligence (AI) technology, the bank’s voice-based customer service tool will be able to understand different accents and pronunciations, as well as everyday language concerning money.

The system, known as the Spending Insights Tool, is being tested with 75% of the NatWest Group’s Royal Bank of Scotland customers.

It has been developed by combining Nvidia’s technology with NatWest’s AI research and customer data. “Together, researchers and engineers from both organisations set out to address a challenge facing the next generation of conversational banking services: improving how speech AI understands the wide range of accents, words, phrases and financial language used across the UK,” said the bank.

Spending Insights allows customers to talk naturally about finances using voice and text. They can ask questions about their spending and receive personalised insights. “Customers can interrupt, ask follow-up questions and provide additional context, with the experience combining conversational responses with interactive charts and visualisations,” said NatWest.

Maja Pantic, chief AI research officer at NatWest Group, said customers can interact with the bank “in a way that feels natural to them”.

“If they choose to speak to AI, the technology needs to understand the different accents, words and everyday language used across the UK,” he added.

According to Aser Blanco, global head of banking at Nvidia, the real-time nature of speech recognition makes it challenging. “Working with NatWest has allowed us to apply Nvidia Nemotron open-source models to those real-world banking challenges and identify where the technology can be improved,” he said. “The results show how adapting speech applications to real-world language can make voice experiences more accurate and natural.”

Nvidia Nemotron automatic speech recognition converts spoken words into text, which is then interpreted by NatWest’s proprietary small language models.

Voice banking is becoming an increased focus for banks, and they are applying AI to the challenge.

title: AI has not invented new attacks, it has removed the waiting
raw_text:
Every year brings the same headline. Attacks are up, breaches are up, and the numbers are worse than 12 months ago. What has changed lately is not the volume so much as the tempo. Artificial intelligence (AI) has lowered the cost of entry for people who want to attack organisations, and it has stripped out much of the waiting that used to sit inside a campaign.

Much of the commentary around AI today conflates capability with deployment. But what a model can do in a laboratory is not necessarily what threat actors are demonstrably doing at scale. The two are worth separating, because the changes showing up in real campaigns are less cinematic than the headlines, but rather more consequential.

The pauses are disappearing

Take capability first. In 2025, Anthropic documented a UK-based operator running a ransomware business who relied on a commercial model for almost every technical step, from building the malware to setting the ransom demand. That operator could not have done the work alone. Skills which took years to acquire can now be rented by the hour.

Malware creation attracts attention, but it is the part organisations should worry about least. AI-written malicious code is still immature and remains recognisable to a competent detection stack. The bigger change is either side of the malware, where the results are much harder to see.

Reconnaissance is the first of those. A Chinese state-linked actor has been observed using models to establish where satellite ground station terminals physically sit, what technology surrounds them and which parts are worth going after, then to generate payload ideas. None of that is an exploit. It is homework, at a pace no research team could match on its own.

The second is what happens after data is taken. In the MOVEit campaign of 2023, the theft was quick, but working out what had been stolen, from whom, and what it was worth stretched on for months, which bought victims time to respond. Handed the same material today, a model answers a question such as “find everything relating to debt, contracts or trade secrets, in any language” in an afternoon. Models are markedly better than traditional tooling at spotting sensitive material in languages other than English, opening them up to victims in global markets.

At a macro scale, attackers are building infrastructure of their own. Open-weight models sit only a few months behind the frontier and run on hardware an operator already owns, using tools such as Ollama. Research from SentinelLabs and Censys found roughly 175,000 exposed Ollama hosts worldwide, outside any platform’s abuse monitoring, and the North Korean group Kimsuky has been seen gathering self-hosting tools and agent development packages. That AI cannot be revoked by a provider.

None of that amounts to a new attack. It is the same attacks with the pauses taken out, and the gaps defenders relied on for time are closing. Matching that pace is now the defensive problem.

The autonomous SOC is a heading, not a purchase

A common instinct for businesses is to point AI at its own estate and find the holes before an attacker does. Offensive self-testing is legitimate, but it generates enormous work for people already stretched repelling today’s attacks. Producing security findings has never been the constraint. Reviewing, verifying, approving and safely deploying them is.

The better starting point is getting faster at the work already in the queue. Triage, enrichment, investigation, drafting and reviewing playbooks. Not every task needs a frontier model either, and routing each one to the cheapest capable model is more useful than chasing the top of a benchmark table.

The autonomous SOC is widely misunderstood here. It is not a product to be bought but a maturity model, and most organisations sit in the middle of it, using AI to assist triage and investigation while people make the decisions. The question is not how autonomous a SOC should be, but whether the organisation retains control over the decisions that matter.

A useful comparison is the flight deck. A pilot does not work every surface of the aircraft by hand. The job is monitoring the systems, applying judgement and remaining accountable, on the loop rather than in it and present for the moments that need a person.

The reason that matters is arithmetic. If the threat landscape sets the pace and the first two steps of an investigation still run on human timescales, the maths does not work. Automate where confidence is highest, keep people where judgement is needed, and build trust between the two deliberately rather than by accident.

Bounded projects, a code audit or a detection rule refresh are sensible places to begin. Done well, the shift moves analysts from operating to orchestrating, and the skills that made them good remain the foundation for what comes next.

Same tools, different discipline

Attackers are using AI in exactly the way legitimate users do. They ask questions, get answers faster than they could find them alone, and act. The advantage will not go to whoever adopts AI first, but to whoever works out what to hand over and what to keep hold of. That decision is better made now than halfway through an incident.
